anubanini-rock-relief.name: Anubanini rock relief
anubanini-rock-relief.summary: A rock relief from around 2300 BC in Kermanshah province, Iran, believed to belong to the Lullubi culture and considered among the earliest rock reliefs of Iran.

lullubi.name: Lullubi
lullubi.summary: A group of Bronze Age tribes from the Zagros Mountains, in what is now Iraqi Kurdistan, who clashed with the Akkadian Empire and Assyria during the 3rd millennium BCE.

kermanshah-province.name: Kermanshah province
kermanshah-province.summary: A province of Iran bordering Iraq, part of the area known as Iranian Kurdistan, with its capital at the city of Kermanshah.

elam.name: Elam
elam.summary: An ancient civilization centered in western and southwestern Iran, one of the leading political forces of the ancient Near East, with written records from around 3000 BCE.

tureng-tepe.name: Tureng Tepe
tureng-tepe.summary: A Neolithic and Chalcolithic archaeological site in northeastern Iran's Gorgan plain, later the site of a major fort on the Sasanian-era 'Alexander's wall.'

jiroft-culture.name: Jiroft culture
jiroft-culture.summary: Early Bronze Age archaeological culture of southeastern Iran, centered near the town of Jiroft, proposed as an independent civilization between Elam and the Indus Valley.

konar-sandal.name: Konar Sandal
konar-sandal.summary: A Bronze Age archaeological site in the Halil River valley just south of Jiroft, in Iran's Kerman Province.

behistun-inscription.name: Behistun inscription
behistun-inscription.summary: A multilingual Achaemenid rock inscription and relief carved for Darius the Great between 522 and 486 BCE, key to deciphering cuneiform as the longest known trilingual inscription.

darius-the-great.name: Darius the Great
darius-the-great.summary: Third King of Kings of the Achaemenid Empire (522–486 BCE), who ruled it at its territorial peak, reorganized it into provinces, and commissioned the Behistun inscription.

lorestan-province.name: Lorestan
lorestan-province.summary: A province in western Iran in the Zagros Mountains, near the Iraqi border, whose capital is Khorramabad.

sarpol-e-zahab.name: Sarpol-e Zahab
sarpol-e-zahab.summary: A city in Kermanshah province, Iran, near Qasr-e Shirin and the Iraqi border, serving as capital of its county and district.

kul-e-farah.name: Kul-e Farah
kul-e-farah.summary: Open-air archaeological sanctuary in Iran's Zagros Mountains, home to six Elamite-era rock reliefs near the town of Izeh.

eshkaft-e-salman.name: Eshkaft-e Salman
eshkaft-e-salman.summary: An archaeological site with Elamite rock reliefs in Khuzestan province, Iran.

enmebaragesi.name: Enmebaragesi
enmebaragesi.summary: Penultimate king of the first dynasty of Kish, around 2750 BC, the earliest ruler on the Sumerian King List confirmed directly by archaeological evidence.

susa.name: Susa
susa.summary: Ancient city in what is now Iran that served as capital of Elam and winter capital of the Achaemenid Empire, remaining strategically important through the Parthian and Sasanian periods.

kurigalzu-ii.name: Kurigalzu II
kurigalzu-ii.summary: 22nd king of the Kassite dynasty of Babylon (c. 1332–1308 BC), placed on the throne by the Assyrian king Aššur-Uballiṭ I; he reigned 25 years before turning on his former allies.

ashur-uballit-i.name: Ashur-uballit I
ashur-uballit-i.summary: King of Assyria from about 1363 to 1328 BC, whose defeat of the Mitanni marked Assyria's rise as a powerful empire and led to early Assyrian intervention in Babylonian affairs.

middle-assyrian-empire.name: Middle Assyrian Empire
middle-assyrian-empire.summary: Assyria's first period as an empire, from about 1363 BC to 912 BC, during which it became the dominant power of northern Mesopotamia.

eannatum.name: Eannatum
eannatum.summary: A Sumerian ruler of Lagash around 2450 BC who built one of the first verifiable empires, subduing Elam, destroying Susa, and dominating Sumer and Akkad.

lugal-anne-mundu.name: Lugal-Anne-Mundu
lugal-anne-mundu.summary: Most important king of the Sumerian city-state of Adab around 2500 BC, said to have reigned 90 years and built what may have been the first empire in recorded history.

manishtushu.name: Manishtushu
manishtushu.summary: Third king of the Akkadian Empire, reigning about 15 years from roughly 2270 to 2255 BCE; son of Sargon the Great and succeeded by his son Naram-Sin, who later deified him.

anshan-persia.name: Anshan
anshan-persia.summary: An ancient Elamite and Persian city in the Zagros Mountains of southwestern Iran, one of the earliest urban states and capitals of Elam from the late 4th millennium BCE.

puzur-inshushinak.name: Puzur-Inshushinak
puzur-inshushinak.summary: King of Elam, last of the Awan dynasty by the Susa kinglist, who died around 2110 BC; the first historical figure in Elamite history.

ka-tilia-u-iv.name: Kaštiliašu IV
ka-tilia-u-iv.summary: The 28th Kassite king of Babylon, ruling around 1232 to 1225 BC, whose war against Assyria ended in a catastrophic defeat.

gudea.name: Gudea
gudea.summary: A Sumerian ruler (ensi) of Lagash in southern Mesopotamia who reigned around 2144–2124 BC, presiding over a golden age of relative independence during the Gutian period.

shulgi.name: Shulgi
shulgi.summary: A king of Ur who reigned 48 years (c. 2094–2046 BC), completed the Great Ziggurat of Ur begun by his father Ur-Nammu, and was later worshipped as a god.

shu-sin.name: Shu-Sin
shu-sin.summary: A king of Sumer and Akkad and the fourth ruler of the Ur III dynasty, who died around 2028 BC after succeeding Amar-Sin, possibly his father.

kidin-hutran.name: Kidin-Hutran
kidin-hutran.summary: A Middle Elamite king of the Igihalkid dynasty known for wars against Babylonia, including raids that deposed Babylonian kings.

enlil-nadin-shumi.name: Enlil-nadin-shumi
enlil-nadin-shumi.summary: King of Babylon around 1224 BC whose reign lasted roughly six months to a year before he was overthrown by an Elamite invasion under Kidin-Hutran III.

adad-shuma-iddina.name: Adad-shuma-iddina
adad-shuma-iddina.summary: 31st king of the Kassite dynasty of Babylon, reigning around 1222–1217 BC, likely as a vassal following Assyrian conquest of Babylonia.

ur.name: Ur
ur.summary: A major Sumerian city-state in ancient Mesopotamia dating from about 3800 BC, whose patron deity was the moon god Nanna and whose ziggurat still stands partially restored.

ibbi-sin.name: Ibbi-Sin
ibbi-sin.summary: The last king of Sumer and Akkad's Ur III dynasty (r. c. 2028–2004 BC), whose empire collapsed under Amorite and Elamite raids until Elam captured Ur and took him prisoner.

sin-mythology.name: Sin (Nanna)
sin-mythology.summary: Mesopotamian god of the moon, also called Nanna, associated with cattle herding, the crescent symbol, and sometimes seen as a judge of the dead.

proto-elamite-script.name: Proto-Elamite script
proto-elamite-script.summary: A largely undeciphered early Bronze Age writing system used briefly before Elamite cuneiform, found at only a handful of sites and resembling contemporary Mesopotamian proto-cuneiform tablets.

sumer.name: Sumer
sumer.summary: The earliest known civilization, in southern Mesopotamia (now south-central Iraq), emerging between the 5th and 4th millennium BCE; its cities produced the world's earliest known written texts.

linear-elamite.name: Linear Elamite
linear-elamite.summary: A writing system used in Elam roughly between 2300 and 1850 BCE, known from a few monumental inscriptions and argued by some to be the oldest purely phonographic script.

tepe-yahya.name: Tepe Yahya
tepe-yahya.summary: A Bronze Age archaeological site in southeastern Iran showing early clay tablet use, early metallurgy and stoneware manufacture.

elamite-cuneiform.name: Elamite cuneiform
elamite-cuneiform.summary: A logo-syllabic writing system used for the Elamite language, known mainly from tablets recording economic transactions, most created during the Achaemenid era.

cuneiform.name: Cuneiform
cuneiform.summary: The earliest known writing system, made of wedge-shaped marks pressed into clay, developed for Sumerian and later adapted for Akkadian and other ancient Near Eastern languages.

susiana.name: Susiana
susiana.summary: Ancient region in southwestern Iran around the city of Susa, forming the core lowland zone of early Elamite civilization and later organized as an Achaemenid satrapy.

sargon-of-akkad.name: Sargon of Akkad
sargon-of-akkad.summary: First ruler of the Akkadian Empire, who conquered Sumeria's city-states in the 24th to 23rd centuries BC and is sometimes seen as history's first emperor; he later became a legendary figure in Assyrian literature.

akkadian-empire.name: Akkadian Empire
akkadian-empire.summary: An ancient kingdom established around 2300 BCE, often considered the first empire in world history, uniting Akkadian and Sumerian speakers across Mesopotamia under Sargon of Akkad and his successors.

naram-sin-of-akkad.name: Naram-Sin
naram-sin-of-akkad.summary: A ruler of Akkad who reigned around 2255–2218 BC, grandson of Sargon, under whom the empire reached its greatest extent and who was the first Mesopotamian king to claim divinity.

awan-dynasty.name: Awan dynasty
awan-dynasty.summary: The first known dynasty of Elam, about which very little survives, dated to roughly 2400 to 2015 BC and centered on a city-state of uncertain location.

third-dynasty-of-ur.name: Third Dynasty of Ur
third-dynasty-of-ur.summary: A Mesopotamian dynasty based in Ur in the 21st century BCE, briefly the region's dominant power; founded by Ur-Namma and expanded into an empire by his son Shulgi before collapsing around 2004 BCE.

shimashki-dynasty.name: Shimashki dynasty
shimashki-dynasty.summary: An early dynasty that ruled the ancient region of Elam, southeast of Babylonia, from about 2100 to 1900 BC, known mainly from a king-list found at Susa.

tepe-sofalin.name: Tepe Sofalin
tepe-sofalin.summary: An ancient Near Eastern site on the Tehran Plain in Iran, occupied from the Late Chalcolithic through the Early Bronze Age and again in the Iron Age, with Proto-Elamite era finds.

tepe-sialk.name: Tepe Sialk
tepe-sialk.summary: A large ancient archaeological site near Kashan in central Iran, linked to the Zayandeh River Culture.

sexagesimal.name: Sexagesimal
sexagesimal.summary: A base-60 number system invented by the ancient Sumerians and passed on to the Babylonians, still used today in modified form for time and angles.

mohenjo-daro.name: Mohenjo-daro
mohenjo-daro.summary: One of the largest cities of the ancient Indus Valley Civilisation, built around 2500 BCE and home to at least 40,000 people before being abandoned by about 1700 BCE.

sukkalmah-dynasty.name: Sukkalmah dynasty
sukkalmah-dynasty.summary: Early dynasty of ancient Elam, in West Asia, that ruled roughly 1900 to 1500 BC and is unusually well documented through cuneiform records from Susa.

kish-sumer.name: Kish
kish-sumer.summary: An important archaeological site in Iraq near ancient Babylon, occupied from the Ubaid period to the Hellenistic period, whose patron deities included Ishtar and later Zababa.

akkad-city.name: Akkad
akkad-city.summary: Capital of the Akkadian Empire, the dominant political power in Mesopotamia for about 150 years in the late 3rd millennium BC; its exact location remains unknown.

kassites.name: Kassites
kassites.summary: A people from the Zagros Mountains who controlled Babylonia under the Kassite dynasty from about 1531 to 1155 BC, ruling first from Babylon and later from Dur-Kurigalzu.

kindattu.name: Kindattu
kindattu.summary: Sixth king of the Shimashki dynasty of Elam, who invaded and conquered Ur around 2004 BC and captured its last king, Ibbi-Sin.

ishbi-erra.name: Ishbi-Erra
ishbi-erra.summary: Founder of the dynasty of Isin in ancient Lower Mesopotamia, reigning from about 2018 to 1985 BC.

indo-iranians.name: Indo-Iranians
indo-iranians.summary: A group of Proto-Indo-European-speaking peoples who spread Indo-Iranian languages across Eurasia from the early 2nd millennium BCE, originating near modern Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan and Tajikistan before splitting into Iranian and Indo-Aryan branches.

zoroaster.name: Zoroaster
zoroaster.summary: Iranian religious reformer traditionally dated to the 7th-6th centuries BC (some scholars place him earlier), who became the spiritual founder of Zoroastrianism through his hymns, the Gathas.

zoroastrianism.name: Zoroastrianism
zoroastrianism.summary: An ancient Iranian religion founded on the teachings of Zoroaster, centred on the deity Ahura Mazda and the choice between truth and chaos, once Greater Iran's dominant faith under the Sassanid Empire.

historical-vedic-religion.name: Historical Vedic religion
historical-vedic-religion.summary: The religious ideas and practices of Indo-Aryan peoples in northwest India during the Vedic period (c. 1500–500 BCE), recorded in Vedic texts and one of the major traditions that shaped modern Hinduism.

ahura-mazda.name: Ahura Mazda
ahura-mazda.summary: The chief god and sky deity of Zoroastrianism, first prominently invoked in the Achaemenid-era Behistun Inscription of Darius the Great.

mithra.name: Mithra
mithra.summary: An ancient Iranian deity of covenants, light, oaths, justice, the sun and friendship, later linked to the Roman god Mithras through Zoroastrian influence.

atar.name: Atar
atar.summary: The Zoroastrian concept of holy fire, regarded as the visible presence of the god Ahura Mazda, with purification rituals performed 1,128 times a year.

daeva.name: Daeva
daeva.summary: In Zoroastrianism, a supernatural being with negative traits, originally described as 'gods to be rejected' in the earliest texts and later seen as promoters of chaos and evil.

magi.name: Magi
magi.summary: Priests of Zoroastrianism and earlier Iranian religions; the term later broadened to mean magicians and, in the Gospel of Matthew, the wise men who visited the infant Jesus.

varuna.name: Varuna
varuna.summary: A Hindu god originally seen as the sovereign ruler of the sky and cosmic moral order in Vedic times, later transformed into the lord of the waters and oceans.

kura-araxes-culture.name: Kura–Araxes culture
kura-araxes-culture.summary: Archaeological culture that existed from about 4000 to 2000 BC across the Caucasus and nearby regions, marked by a sedentary agricultural economy and named after the Kura and Araxes river valleys.

lake-van.name: Lake Van
lake-van.summary: Turkey's largest lake, a saline soda lake in the Armenian highlands with no outlet, formed after a volcanic eruption blocked its original drainage.

uruk-period.name: Uruk period
uruk-period.summary: The era, roughly 4000 to 3100 BC, when the first cities and states arose in Mesopotamia, named after the city of Uruk where innovations like the potter's wheel appeared.

yanik-tepe.name: Yanik Tepe culture
yanik-tepe.summary: A local variant of the Kura–Araxes culture, named for a Chalcolithic and Bronze Age site in Iranian Azerbaijan near Lake Urmia.

lake-urmia.name: Lake Urmia
lake-urmia.summary: A salt lake in Iranian Azerbaijan that was once one of the world's largest saltwater lakes but has shrunk drastically from drought and damming.

boris-kuftin.name: Boris Kuftin
boris-kuftin.summary: A Soviet archaeologist and ethnographer (1892–1953) who discovered the Trialeti culture in the 1930s and coined the term Kura-Araxes in 1940.

shengavit-site.name: Shengavit
shengavit-site.summary: A Bronze Age archaeological site near Yerevan, Armenia, inhabited from about 3000 to 2500 BCE, and a type site for the Kura-Araxes culture.
